posts.cooked:
Katana is a good product for manufacturing-adjacent workflows, but if you’re not doing actual production/BOM management, it’s overkill. That friction compounds over time, and it sounds like you’ve hit the wall with it.

Prediko (~$59-119/mo) is probably your best bet if you’re primarily on Shopify. Native integration, solid PO workflow, demand-based replenishment that actually forecasts instead of just pinging you when stock is low. Multi-store works at higher tiers. Where it falls short is anything beyond Shopify – Amazon, eBay, Walmart sync is limited.

If overselling across channels is the main fire you’re putting out, Stock Sync plus Shopify’s native POs (~$20-40/mo combined) gets the job done. You’d handle replenishment triggers manually or with a spreadsheet. Not glamorous. Works fine if your catalog isn’t huge.

Linnworks and Brightpearl are the “complete” answers, but at $449+/mo with onboarding that feels like an ERP implementation, they’re probably exactly what you’re trying to get away from.

Honestly, the $40-120/mo range for multi-channel sync with intelligent replenishment is pretty bare right now. Most tools nail one or two of those pieces but not all three at SMB pricing. That’s been shifting fast since Stocky got sunset, so it’s worth rechecking every few months.

What’s your SKU count, and which channels are you on beyond Shopify? That matters more than anything else here.

Curious what you’re looking for specifically in a PO app?

posts.cooked:
Lots of good app suggestions here already, been researching this space myself lately, so I’ll add the evaluation side instead. Part of why this search is hard: “complete inventory management” is really two different problems. Multi-store sync has to be event-driven (react to every order in real time), while replenishment planning is batch analysis over history. Most apps are built around one and retrofit the other.

Three things I’d check in any demo before committing:

  1. Is the sync webhook-driven or polling? If it polls every 5–15 min, your other channels are blind in that window – which is exactly when oversells happen on a busy day.

  2. Real per-location support, or just one aggregate number?

  3. What happens on a refund or a cancelled order – does stock actually come back automatically?

The answers to those three will tell you more than the feature comparison pages.

Hi @woysanstore

If your biggest pain point is keeping inventory synchronized across multiple Shopify stores without moving to a full ERP, you might want to take a look at Easify Inventory Sync

The app focuses specifically on inventory synchronization, making it a good fit if you already have your sales channels set up but need a simpler way to keep stock accurate.

With Inventory Groups, you can link products that represent the same physical inventory across multiple Shopify stores. Once they’re connected, any sale or manual inventory adjustment in one store is automatically reflected in the others in real time, helping prevent overselling and eliminating the need for manual stock updates.

I like this approach because it stays focused on solving the inventory sync problem without adding the complexity of a full ERP system. If inventory synchronization is the main reason you’re looking to move away from Katana, it could be a solution worth considering.

That said, if purchase orders and replenishment planning are also essential parts of your workflow, you may still want to pair Easify Inventory Sync with a dedicated purchasing or inventory planning solution, depending on how advanced your requirements are.

Hope this helps, and if you have any questions about how Inventory Groups work, Easify’s support team is always happy to help

posts.cooked: Not a fit for multi-store/marketplace sync specifically (that’s a different problem than what I’ve focused on), but on the “complete inventory management combines two different needs” point someone raised — that’s exactly right, and worth keeping separate in your evaluation. Event-driven sync (Stock Sync, Easify) and batch replenishment forecasting (Prediko, DemandMind) are genuinely different engineering problems, and a lot of “complete” tools are actually just bolting one onto the other. Might be worth picking the best tool for each rather than one that claims both.

I’d evaluate this as two separate workflows rather than one feature checklist. For multi-store and marketplace sync, use a few representative SKUs and test whether an order, refund, cancellation, and manual adjustment update every relevant location quickly enough to prevent oversells. For replenishment, test whether the tool produces a reviewable reorder list from sales, stock on hand, lead times, and safety stock, then lets you turn that list into a PO you can check before exporting. That makes it easier to see whether one tool genuinely fits both jobs or whether sync and purchasing need separate tools.

Skubase promotion: I work with Skubase. It supports the planning side with reorder recommendations and supplier purchase orders that can be exported as Excel files. It is not presented as a replacement for unverified multi-store or marketplace sync. Skubase is not yet listed in the Shopify App Store.

Would you be interested in seeing what Skubase recommends for your store?

**Quick test for any reorder tool:** make a PO, then ask it for suggestions again before that PO arrives.

If the same quantity comes back, it’s ignoring stock that’s already on order. With a long lead time, that’s a double order.

Disclosure: I build EZStock. It does purchase orders and reorder suggestions, not stock sync between stores or marketplaces, so you’d pair it with one of the sync apps above.

Suggestions come from your sales history, minus what’s already on open POs, rounded up to case packs. Each one shows its working: “Sells 2.3 a day (last 365 days) × 60 days = 138, minus 42 in stock”.

POs get emailed to the supplier straight from the app. Suggestions are on the $49 plan; the free plan has reorder points and 5 POs a month.

posts.cooked:
@woysanstore, it’s been a few months since you posted, so you may have sorted this already. If not, here’s one way to look at it.

What you described is really three jobs: (1) syncing stock across your Shopify stores and marketplaces, (2) purchase orders, and (3) replenishment planning. Most “all-in-one” tools are strong at one of these and stretched on the other two. That’s often why something like Katana starts to feel heavy: you’re paying the manufacturing-ERP cost of setting it up just to get #3.

A setup that tends to stay light:

  • Use a dedicated sync tool for #1. This one needs to be fast and event-based, so don’t build it yourself.
  • Use Shopify’s native purchase orders for #2. They’re much better than they were six months ago.
  • Do #3 off combined sales from every channel. This is the part most tools get wrong when you sell in several places. Each SKU needs its total demand across all stores, plus its seasonality, supplier lead time and stock already on order. Otherwise you under-order the products that sell mostly on marketplaces.

Disclosure: I build custom replenishment dashboards for multichannel brands, so take this with that in mind. I’m not selling an app subscription. It’s a fixed-price build around how you actually sell. If it would help, I’m happy to show you a demo with reorder dates per SKU that account for lead times, the cash needed each month, and “what if demand drops 20%” scenarios.

Happy to compare notes here or by DM if it’s useful. And if you’ve already found something that works, I’d genuinely like to hear what you went with.

A Shopify merchant is looking to replace Katana, which feels too complex or poorly suited to selling across multiple Shopify stores and other marketplaces. Their goal is a lighter solution combining inventory sync, purchase orders (POs), and replenishment planning, but replies note that few affordable tools handle all three well.

Suggestions include Brightpearl and Linnworks as more complete but potentially ERP-like options; Sumtracker for multi-store sync and POs; and Prediko or DemandMind for forecasting and reorder planning. Stock Sync, Easify, and Shopify’s native POs were proposed as simpler combinations. Several contributors recommend treating real-time stock synchronization and sales-based replenishment as separate workflows, possibly using different tools. A later reply stresses that forecasts should account for combined demand across channels, supplier lead times, and stock already on open POs.

To evaluate options, commenters advise testing how orders, refunds, cancellations, and manual adjustments sync, and whether reorder suggestions account for existing POs and can be reviewed before creating one. No product choice or final resolution is reported; the merchant’s SKU count and specific marketplaces remain unanswered.
